result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.minimum_cycle_basis()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a minimum weight cycle basis for the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L12097-L12185){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.minimum_cycle_basis(weight=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Minimum cycle basis](/assets/graphs/minimum-cycle-basis.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The house-shaped graph again. Its minimum cycle basis is the triangle A, C, B (length 3, accent color) and the square B, C, E, D (length 4, teal), sharing edge B to C; the card totals 7, the smallest possible for two independent cycles." width="100%"} A minimum cycle basis is a cycle basis where the sum of weights of all cycles is minimized. For unweighted graphs, this minimizes the sum of cycle lengths. This implements a variant of Horton's algorithm: 1. for each edge `(u,v)`, find the shortest path from `u` to `v` not using `(u,v)` 2. this gives a candidate cycle for each edge 3. sort candidates by weight and greedily select linearly independent cycles ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edge attribute name to use as weight. If `None`, uses the default edge weight (or `1.0` if edges don't have weights). The algorithm finds the basis that minimizes the sum of cycle weights. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A list of cycles forming a minimum weight cycle basis. Each cycle is a list of node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on a directed graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Horton's algorithm (1987) generates a candidate cycle for every edge $e = (u, v)$ by routing the shortest $u \to v$ path in $G \setminus e$ back through $e$, then greedily selects the lightest cycles that are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_2$. That independence check is the expensive step and pushes the total cost to $O(E \cdot V^2)$. The total *weight* of the resulting basis is unique even when the basis itself is not: multiple bases can tie for minimum weight, and this call returns one of them. Disconnected graphs are handled per component. When edge weights are irrelevant, `cycle_basis()` is substantially faster. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two triangles sharing an edge form the minimum-weight basis here, since together they cover every cycle in the graph at the lowest possible total length: ::: {#edc2e93e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Two triangles sharing an edge graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "A") .add_edge("B", "D") .add_edge("D", "C") ) basis = graph.minimum_cycle_basis() len(basis) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: Passing `weight=` minimizes total edge weight instead of edge count. A single triangle only has one possible cycle, so it's returned regardless of weights: ::: {#4c4bc042 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=1.0) .add_edge("B", "C", weight=2.0) .add_edge("C", "A", weight=3.0) ) graph.minimum_cycle_basis(weight="weight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [[1, 3, 2]] ``` ::: :::
